background.definition: Gangrene is defined as the death of tissue, usually secondary to impaired or absent blood flow. Dry, wet, and gas gangrene are the major forms. Dry gangrene develops slowly over time and is marked by the gradual loss of blood flow causing the skin to dry up and flake off. In wet gangrene the skin is moist and frequently infected with bacteria, and the gangrene may spread rapidly. Gas gangrene spreads quickly, is frequently fatal, and is usually caused by anaerobic bacteria, most commonly the Clostridia species. Other types of gangrene are internal gangrene involving one or more organs including the appendix, gall bladder, or bowel. Fournier's gangrene is a form of necrotizing fasciitis involving the anogenital region.

list.listitem: Approximately 15% of the more than 150 million people with diabetes worldwide will at some point develop diabetic foot ulcerations that may lead to gangrene.
Any process that obstructs the blood supply to an organ or tissue may result in gangrene.

Examples include vascular degenerative changes such as diabetes or atherosclerosis, inflammatory processes such as Raynaud's disease, physical injuries such as frostbite or trauma, and emboli to arteries such as in subacute bacterial endocarditis or accidental arterial injections.
Infectious agents, especially Clostridium perfringens, an anaerobic gram-positive, spore-forming bacilli, are the causative agents in gas gangrene.
Other infectious agents involved in wet gangrene include streptococcal or staphylococcal species.
See Risk Factors table.
When blood flow to tissue is obstructed, tissues may undergo necrosis and may become secondarily infected.

In gas gangrene, the causative organism is Clostridium perfringens. These bacteria may enter the skin at a surgical or traumatic wound site where they release several exotoxins, the most important being alpha-toxin, which hydrolyses cell membranes, causing tissue necrosis, inactivation of leukocytes, and hemolysis of red blood cells.

A Cochrane review evaluating screening asymptomatic people for peripheral arterial disease (PAD) found no RCTs on the subject. Similarly, the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) found insufficient evidence to recommend performing ankle-brachial index (ABI) to screen asymptomatic individuals for PAD. B

The American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) recommends obtaining ABI on patients with symptoms or physical findings suggestive of PAD (eg, abnormal pedal pulses, nonhealing lower extremity wound or gangrene). B

AHA/ACC recommends counseling patients with PAD and diabetes to perform self-foot exam, practice healthy foot behaviors, and undergo biannual foot exam through their physician. All patients with PAD should seek immediate care with the development of any foot infection to minimize tissue loss or development of gangrene. C

list.listitem: Dry gangrene: local erythema, brown-black discoloration, locally cold and numb, skin is hard and dry in texture, clear demarcation between viable and necrotic tissue. Patient may give a history of focal pain.

Wet gangrene: edema, blistering, numbness, oozing, and a foul smelling odor. Frequently follows a traumatic injury to the area in diabetics, secondary to sensory loss. Spreads rapidly and may be fatal. Usually involves a bacterial infection.

Gas gangrene: the most dangerous form of gangrene. Affected area will show gas bubbles in the skin, pale gray discoloration, may not bleed when cut, may be extremely edematous and painful, and patient may have a high fever and appear systemically ill.
Obtain CBC; elevated white blood cell count may indicate infection. Culture the site to determine infectious agents, including culture for anaerobes. Blood cultures may reveal systemic spread.

Consider biopsy for signs of cell death if diagnosis is in question. Histopathology may reveal a noninfectious inflammatory process or coexisting condition such as collagen vascular disease or vasculitis.
Obtain serum glucose and HbA1c to determine risk for diabetes and to aid glucose management.

Consider noninvasive testing such as ankle-brachial index (ABI) and doppler exam to evaluate for peripheral vascular disease. Arteriogram may visualize the patency of arteries if noninvasive testing is nondiagnostic.
Obtain radiographs to reveal pockets of gas in the superficial tissues that are not readily palpable on physical exam in the case of gas gangrene.
Obtain MRI to determine involvement of muscle or fat, or both, and thus the depth and extent of disease.

Consider gangrene in patients with edema, discoloration, odor, or numbness, especially if they are over age 50, are diabetic, or have peripheral vascular disease. If the gangrene occurred suddenly, consider gas gangrene as a potential cause.
The lower extremity is the most common location. If the gangrene is located in the upper extremities, consider Raynaud's disease or other collagen vascular diseases as a potential etiology.

Assess peripheral vasculature by measuring distal pulses and capillary refill. If there is sudden onset loss of peripheral pulses, consider arterial emboli. If there is gradual onset, consider atherosclerosis, diabetes, or other chronic vascular diseases.

Immediately hospitalize patients who present with wet or gas gangrene and consult a specialist competent in treating vascular diseases as this is a medical emergency and local wound care alone is not adequate. C
Rapidly initiate empiric antibiotic therapy for any case where primary or secondary infection is suspected. C
Aggressive, serial debridement of the wound is the mainstay of treatment, especially for wet and gas gangrene. Incision and drainage alone is not an appropriate surgical strategy. C
Surgical amputation of the digit, extremity, or limb as dictated by the extent of disease should be reserved as a last resort but may be necessary. C

For wet and gas gangrene, appropriate antibiotics should be based on culture and sensitivities once available. However, immediate empiric therapy with broad-spectrum antibiotics should be started without delay (e.g., vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam or carbapenem).

In cases of dry gangrene, several investigational limb salvage therapies have been explored. Gene therapy, which involves injecting genes of proteins that facilitate auto-revascularization of affected extremities, may hasten wound healing but does not appear to improve major amputation, amputation-free survival, and all-cause mortality. Oral or systemic prostanoids like prostacyclins and prostaglandins may modestly improve ulcer healing and pain from ischemia, but do not alter amputation rates, cardiovascular death, and may cause adverse events. Autologous cell-based therapies involving bone marrow and peripheral blood stem cells do not appear to hasten healing of ischemic ulcers. Growth factors have unclear benefits for ischemic ulcers and pain. Low quality evidence with high risk of bias suggests they may improve amputation rates (OR 0.99; 95% CI 0.71-1.38). It is still unclear if autologous platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is helpful in the treatment of gangrene.

Vasodilating agents in patients with proven atherosclerosis may be helpful in early cases. However, a systematic review of naftidrofuryl for patients with critical limb ischemia found only a few small RCTs of limited quality (8 studies with 269 patients), and no clear evidence of treatment benefit.
In cases with proven emboli, thrombolytic agents may be helpful in the early stages.
Supportive care may include fluids, nutritional support, and pain medications.
Aggressive and repetitive excisional debridement of the wound is the mainstay of treatment, especially for wet or gas gangrene.
Incision and drainage alone is not an appropriate surgical strategy.
Surgical amputation of the digit, extremity, or limb as dictated by the extent of disease should be reserved as a last resort but may be necessary.

For patients with severe peripheral arterial disease and critical limb ischemia, revascularization should be considered prior to amputation of gangrenous tissue. Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty is associated with lower peri-procedural complications and shorter hospitalization compared to bypass surgery and should be especially considered for high risk surgical candidates and those with significant comorbidities. However, bypass surgery has better patency rates at 1 year, but not at 4 years. Most other important outcomes appear comparable (eg, mortality, clinical improvement, amputation rates, reintervention rates, quality of life).

In selected cases, the use of maggots (sterile larvae of Lucilia sericata) may provide biologic debridement of necrotic wounds. Maggots are natural removers of necrotic and infected tissue and are even capable of destroying bacteria while leaving healthy tissue unharmed. However, definitive evidence is lacking to support the safety and effectiveness of larval debridement for patients with gangrene.
Early and late rehabilitation after amputation are very important for patient morbidity and mortality.
Consider referral for counseling for patients with concerns about disfigurement from the gangrene itself or from resultant amputation.

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) may inhibit clostridial growth and arrest alpha-toxin production in gas gangrene. However, a Cochrane review for interventions to treat gas gangrene found insufficient evidence for the efficacy of topical HBOT.

Artificial carbon dioxide foot bathing may improve subcutaneous microcirculation especially in patients with peripheral arterial disease. However, studies that demonstrate important patient-oriented outcomes are lacking (eg, decreased amputation rates, mortality, etc.).
Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty is a safe, feasible, and effective procedure as limb sparing treatment in gangrene caused by vascular disease.
There is insufficient evidence to support the efficacy of programs aimed at caring for the contralateral leg of patients who have had a major amputation of the lower extremity.
Spinal cord stimulation may be beneficial while lumbar sympathectomy have uncertain benefits for pain management in patients with critical limb ischemia with nonreconstructable PAD.

Immediately hospitalize patients who present with wet or gas gangrene and consult a specialist competent in treating vascular diseases as this is a medical emergency and local wound care alone is not adequate.

Patients with dry gangrene may be managed as outpatients with close follow-up and immediate hospitalization for progression of disease, but may need hospitalization if extensive surgical treatment becomes necessary.
Prognosis depends on several factors: part of body involved, underlying medical conditions of the patient, extent of the disease, and the early institution of appropriate treatment. C
Dry gangrene has the best prognosis when there is no secondary infection, followed by wet gangrene, with gas gangrene having the worst prognosis. C

Around 10% of patients with minor lower extremity amputation due to diabetes and peripheral arterial disease will go on to have an ipsilateral major amputation within a year; 50% will die in 5 years. B
Approximately 6% and 12% of patients with PAD who undergo a major lower limb amputation will eventually have a contralateral lower limb amputation in 1 and 5 years, respectively. B
If untreated, dry gangrene will progress slowly in a proximal fashion and may require a larger amputation.
If untreated, wet and gas gangrene will progress proximally more rapidly, and may prove fatal secondary to overwhelming sepsis.
Prognosis depends on several factors: part of body involved, underlying medical conditions of the patient, extent of the disease, and the early institution of appropriate treatment.
Dry gangrene has a better prognosis if there is no secondary infection.
Wet gangrene has a poor prognosis because of the rapid spread of infection, which may cause systemic disease and death.
Gas gangrene has the worst prognosis due to anaerobic infection. If not treated early, it can progress to delirium, coma, septic shock, and death.
Follow-up angiography is recommended for revascularization procedures as arterial patency is essential in critical limb ischemia.
Patients should see a physician if they have a persistent fever, discoloration of skin, a wound that is slow to heal, recurring sores, or foul-smelling odor from a wound.
Patients with diabetes or peripheral vascular disease should make proper foot care a priority.
